title: India Faces Ticking Clock on GCAP Entry as Leonardo CEO Sets Deadline
excerpt: With the Franco-German FCAS programme collapsed and a £4.6 billion contract secured, Leonardo's CEO says any new partner must commit within a year — putting pressure on India's sixth-generation fighter ambitions.
body:
• Leonardo CEO Lorenzo Mariani said at Farnborough Airshow that any new country must join GCAP by mid-2027 at the latest, citing the programme's 2035 deadline.
  • India's Chief of Defence Staff confirmed in March 2026 that the Indian Air Force is evaluating entry into either GCAP or the now-collapsed FCAS programme.
  • A £4.6 billion contract awarded to Edgewing in July marks GCAP's transition into full-scale design, raising the stakes for potential new entrants.
  • India's decision hinges on balancing its indigenous AMCA programme with the urgent need to close a widening fighter squadron gap against China.

Leonardo CEO Lorenzo Mariani has drawn a hard line on the timeline for new countries to join the Global Combat Air Programme, the trilateral sixth-generation fighter jet effort backed by the United Kingdom, Italy, and Japan. Speaking at the Farnborough Airshow on July 22, Mariani said any nation eyeing membership must commit by the end of 2026 or, at most, within 12 months.

"My personal opinion — 2026, maximum one year from now," Mariani told Reuters, stressing that while the decision rested with the three partner governments, industry needed clarity to meet the programme's 2035 service target.

The warning carries particular weight for India, which confirmed earlier this year that it is actively evaluating membership in one of Europe's two competing sixth-generation fighter programmes.

India's Sixth-Generation Dilemma

On March 18, India's Chief of Defence Staff General Anil Chauhan informed the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Defence that the Indian Air Force was seeking to join either GCAP or the Future Combat Air System (FCAS), the Franco-German-Spanish alternative. A parliamentary panel subsequently recommended the government evaluate both options, citing the potential to accelerate India's access to AI-enabled warfare systems, advanced sensors, and manned-unmanned teaming capabilities.

That calculus has shifted significantly since March. The Franco-German FCAS programme collapsed in June 2026 over unresolved disputes between Dassault Aviation and Airbus on workshare and intellectual property, effectively eliminating one of India's two options. While India has since explored a bilateral sixth-generation collaboration with France, no formal programme has materialised.

GCAP, by contrast, is accelerating. On July 3, the GCAP Agency awarded a £4.6 billion ($6.14 billion) contract to Edgewing — the joint venture between BAE Systems, Leonardo, and Japan Aircraft Industrial Enhancement — to advance the fighter into detailed design and development. The contract followed Britain's commitment of £8.6 billion over four years to the programme.

The Squadron Gap India Cannot Ignore

India's interest in a sixth-generation partnership stems from a blunt operational reality. The Indian Air Force operates roughly 29 fighter squadrons against an authorised strength of 42 — a shortfall that shows no sign of closing quickly. The retirement of ageing MiG-21s, delays in Tejas Mk1A deliveries, and a stalled multi-role fighter acquisition have all constrained replenishment.

Meanwhile, China now fields two operational stealth fighters — the J-20 and J-35 — and is testing two sixth-generation prototypes, the J-36 and J-50. Indian planners recognise that even the indigenous Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA), a fifth-plus generation stealth fighter with a first flight targeted for 2029, will not address the long-term challenge posed by Chinese sixth-generation platforms.

"There is such pressure and such direction from our three governments to keep the timing strict and to deliver that I think we will find a way to accommodate [new partners] not jeopardising the final timeline."

— Marco Zoff, CEO of Edgewing

What GCAP Offers — and What It Demands

GCAP is designed as a networked combat system integrating a crewed stealth fighter with autonomous drones, AI-driven decision-making, and advanced sensor fusion. The programme's architecture allows participants varying levels of involvement, a flexibility demonstrated when Canada signed on as an observer on July 21.

For India, the potential benefits are substantial: access to cutting-edge aerospace technology, interoperability with key Western allies, and cost-sharing on a programme estimated at tens of billions of dollars. But participation would require navigating complex negotiations on technology transfer, intellectual property, and indigenous manufacturing — issues the parliamentary panel flagged as critical to India's strategic interests.

Germany is also weighing GCAP membership following the FCAS collapse, and Saudi Arabia has long expressed interest. Mariani noted that Germany's existing collaboration on the Eurofighter Typhoon with the UK and Italy made it a natural fit, though he added that Saudi interest also remained.

What Comes Next

Edgewing CEO Marco Zoff has said GCAP's 2035 timeline will not slip even if new partners join, and that any expansion would be a "net positive." The focus now is on completing the concept assessment phase by the end of 2027.

For India, the clock is running. Mariani's deadline means New Delhi has a narrowing window to decide whether to pursue GCAP membership, continue developing a bilateral track with France, or rely solely on the indigenous AMCA. With the FCAS option gone and China advancing rapidly, the strategic pressure to act is mounting.
nri_angle: Indian defence professionals and aerospace engineers in the UK, Italy, and Japan could see expanded career opportunities if India joins GCAP, while the programme's outcome will shape the fighter jets defending Indian airspace for decades.
